summary.text: 系 is traditionally explained as silk threads gathered or connected, suggesting binding and connection. Its early graphic form is disputed: one account sees a hand holding silk; another reads 糸 plus a sound element.

formation.text: Disputed. An account of oracle-bone and bronze forms interprets the graph as a hand holding connected silk, expressing binding or connection. The received Shuowen analysis instead parses 糸 as the thread element and 丿 as phonetic; another proposal links 系 to 攣. The supplied seal-script glyph is a modern redraw and does not settle the competing analyses or their sequence.

components.text: The upper visible stroke is 丿. In the received analysis it is phonetic; another interpretation treats it as a reduced 爪, part of a hand holding silk. These accounts conflict, and the component’s identity is unresolved.

sound_limitation.text: The received account assigns 丿 a sound role, but the competing graphic analysis identifies it as a reduced hand. Although readings are listed for 丿 and 系, the supplied evidence does not resolve the component’s identity or establish their historical sound relation.

sound.text: Modern Mandarin readings are piě for 丿 and xì for 系. This pair does not establish the disputed historical phonetic analysis.

components.text: 糸 is associated with thread. It is the thread element in the received analysis and the silk held by the hand in the alternative pictorial account.

history.text: The oracle-bone and bronze forms are interpreted as a hand holding connected silk. The received Shuowen parsing and a separate proposal linking 系 to 攣 differ from this account. The supplied seal-script glyph is a modern redraw, not a dated artifact, and does not establish a sequence of forms.

系 is explicitly identified as a sound element in 係. The related graphs 系, 係, and 繫 appear as counterparts or variants in some records, but the evidence does not establish one graphic chronology or show that 系 regularly arose by simplifying 繫.

Reported early uses include ritual and place or state names, as well as a bronze personal name. A Warring States text is also reported to use 系 for 奚; the evidence here does not supply the older word’s sound or establish why the graph was used.

uncertainties.text: The proposed hand-and-silk picture, the received analysis of 糸 plus phonetic 丿, and the proposed link to 攣 remain competing accounts of 系’s graphic origin.
The inscriptions cited for ritual, place or state, and personal-name uses are not dated here as attestations of the lexical meanings thread, connection, lineage, or system.
The readings cited for 系 and 係 support a documented phonetic role for 系 in 係, but the distinct reconstructed forms do not resolve the precise historical sound relation.

senses.text: Thread is a recorded gloss and fits the interpretation of silk held by a hand. The evidence does not identify it as the earliest attested lexical use.
Binding or connection is the proposed sense of the hand holding connected silk. This is an interpretation of the graph’s origin, not a dated earliest use.

senses.period: historical; cited in a Han-dynasty text
senses.text: Connection is proposed to have extended to lineage; a Han-dynasty example is cited. The intervening semantic history is not documented.
System is a recorded modern gloss. Its historical development is not shown here.

senses.gloss: use of 系 to write 奚
senses.text: A Warring States use of 系 for 奚 is reported. This is use of the graph to write another word, not a semantic development from 系; the sound comparison is not supplied.

developments.text: An extension from connection to lineage is proposed and illustrated with a Han-dynasty example, but intermediate stages are not documented.

limitations.text: The reported ritual, place or state, and personal-name uses are not established here as dated attestations of the listed lexical senses.
No chronology or semantic development for the modern gloss system is supplied.

overview.text: 系 (xì) is used for thread, connection, lineage, and system. One proposed origin pictures a hand holding connected silk, suggesting binding; another analysis treats 糸 as thread and 丿 as a sound element.

components.text: The upper stroke is read as a sound element in one account and as part of a hand in another; the graph’s origin remains disputed.
糸 represents thread in one analysis and silk in the proposed picture of a hand holding connected strands.

relationships.text: 系 is explicitly treated as a sound element in 係. Both have modern Mandarin reading xì; the supplied Baxter–Sagart rows give 系 MC hejH, OC *[m]-kˤek-s and 係 MC kejH, OC *kˤek-s. The documented role is clear, but the different reconstructed forms do not settle the precise historical sound relation.
Some records describe related or interchangeable uses of 系 and 係, but the timing and extent of this relationship are not established. This character-level relation does not make 人 a component of 系.
Records list 系 as a counterpart or variant of 繫, while another account proposes simplification from 繫. The evidence does not settle their chronology or establish regular simplification.
